name: Tanning drops (Isle of Paradise style)

lead: Tanning drops are concentrated self-tanning products added to your own lotion or skincare so colour deepens with the amount used. Isle of Paradise is one brand associated with the format. The appeal is a custom-shade glow without sun.

The chain is chemical: self-tanners generally rely on DHA, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type browning reaction, with no UV or melanin involved. The colour appears within hours and builds over days. No clinical studies of the format were found.

paras: People mix a few drops into their usual moisturiser, serum or body lotion, adding more for a deeper result, and apply it as they would normally. Colour builds gradually with repeated use.

DHA colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days, and misapplication can produce orange or splotchy results. Skin may be more UV-susceptible for about 24 hours after DHA use, and contact dermatitis is reported.

web.title: How Isle of Paradise Glow Drops Became a Go-To Product During the Pandemic (sponsored)

angle.text: You mix self-tan drops into your moisturiser to choose how deep and how gradual a tan looks, building colour over days. DHA colours the outer skin layer without UV. The colour change is visible within hours.

lead: Tanning drops are concentrated sunless tanning products designed to be mixed into a moisturiser, serum or other skincare so the user can choose how deep the colour goes. The format is associated with brands such as Isle of Paradise, whose self-tanning drops went viral on TikTok around 2020.[1]

People use them to look tanned without UV exposure: adding drops to a face or body moisturiser gives a gradual, adjustable colour that can make skin look healthier and more even, and, as one looksmax.org poster puts it, can make eye and hair colour stand out more.[2]

Sunless tanners usually contain dihydroxyacetone (DHA) at about 3 to 5 percent, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer; the colour is temporary and does not involve melanin or UV.[3] No clinical studies on tanning drops were found.
infobox: Isle of Paradise (founder Jules Von Hep)

paras: The product is added to a base moisturiser, so the amount used affects how deep the colour builds. Gradual tanning lotions in which colour builds with repeated use are a related format.[3] Isle of Paradise's founder, Jules Von Hep, is described as a celebrity spray tan artist.[1]
DHA's browning reaction occurs in the outermost dead skin layer through a Maillard-type reaction and is independent of UV.[3] Erythrulose acts similarly but develops more slowly.[3]

A sponsored 2020 article in Glossy described Isle of Paradise as a two-year-old brand that had ranked first among self-tanning brands at Sephora and sold over a quarter of a million self-tanning drops in six months, with TikTok users' glow-up videos credited for much of the attention. The article is brand-sponsored and its claims are not independently verified.[1]

A looksmax.org thread suggests mixing face tanning drops into moisturiser before bed to wake up with a glow, saying the colour makes blue eyes and blonde hair stand out more and advising barrier cream around the hairline and eyebrows to avoid orange staining. Replies ask which product the poster uses and whether a darker face than body looks unnatural.[2]

The US FDA has approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes, on lips or mucous membranes, or by inhalation.[3] Skin is reported to be more susceptible to UV for about 24 hours after DHA, and DHA can cause contact dermatitis; sunscreen in tanners may fade before the colour does.[3]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, face tanning drops are mentioned as a simple way to add glow, with replies asking about brands and realism.[2]

claims.claim: Mixing tanning drops into night moisturiser makes the face look better by morning.
A darker face than body looks fake.

timeline.event: Sponsored coverage reports Isle of Paradise self-tanning drops topping Sephora's self-tanning category.[1]
